title: Palaces of pearls
hook: if I had palaces of pearls and jewels, may I never forget You (Sri Rag M1, ang 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad, and your line: a hymn for every moment. What song came into your head on its own? Today, the first hymn of this stretch, and it begins in a dream house. Day six hundred forty-seven.

A real estate app, late at night. Infinity pool. Floor-to-ceiling windows over the ocean. A kitchen bigger than a whole apartment, a garden, room for everyone you love. Scroll, imagine, almost smell the sea air. Guru Nanak built a dream house too, in words. Near the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib's main body, in Sri Rag, he raises a palace wall by jeweled wall. And then he asks one question about it.
screen: `A REAL ESTATE APP AT MIDNIGHT.` → `GURU NANAK BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE.` → `THEN ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The shabad is on ang 14. It begins, in effect: if I had a palace built of pearls, inlaid with jewels, its walls plastered with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, a joy to come home to. Then the turn: let it not be that, seeing all this, I go astray, forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind. Then the refrain, the rahao, the line tradition treats as the hymn's center: without the Lord my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place. And then he does it again, three more times, each one bigger. If the floor were paved with diamonds and rubies, and a beautiful companion waited on a jeweled bed. If I became a siddha, a yogi with miraculous powers, appearing and vanishing at will. If I became a sultan, raising armies, sitting on a throne, giving orders. Each time, the same ending: let me not forget You. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say palaces are evil, or that beauty is a trap, or that the rich are lost. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to give up homes, families or work; the Gurus lived as householders. The danger he names is narrower and sharper: forgetting. A beautiful thing can fill the view so completely that the Giver drops out of the picture. The hymn doesn't ask for less. It asks to remember, even with more. And it was put in Sri Rag, a raag tradition associates with evening and with seriousness. A grave melody for a dream house.
screen: `A PALACE OF PEARLS AND MUSK.` · `LEST I FORGET YOU.` · `JEWELS, POWERS, A THRONE.` · `NOT RENUNCIATION: REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Picture your dream house. Really build it: the view, the kitchen, the light in the morning, whoever you'd want there with you. Enjoy it for a few breaths. You're allowed. Then ask Guru Nanak's question: in that house, would I still remember what matters most? Would I still call my mother, still sit quietly, still notice the person who cleans the pool? Then let the house go, gently, like setting down a heavy box. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let go. The bell holds the time.
Palaces of pearls. Guru Nanak imagines every luxury and power, and asks only this: that none of it make him forget the One.
Your line: may I not forget. Today, when you see something you want, a house, a car, a phone, say the line once before you scroll on. Day six hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, that without the Lord the soul burns and there is no other place, is often the line congregations repeat.

fork.setup: you're offered a palace of pearls, walls of musk and sandalwood. what does Guru Nanak ask for?
options: that it not make him forget You.
fork.reveal: he neither grabs nor refuses. he asks to keep remembering the One even with everything.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pearl; the hymn opens with a palace built of pearls.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn against wealth.
what it means: a hymn against forgetting; wealth, beauty and power are dangerous only if they push out the Name.
what a scholar hears: the four-stanza escalation (palace, jeweled bed, siddhi powers, sultanate) uses the rahao as the hymn's thesis, a pattern Guru Nanak uses in other Sri Rag shabads too.

sources.ref: Sri Rag M1, Ang 14 (moti ta mandar oosareh)

notes: The shabad is paraphrased; confirm the four stanzas as summarized (palace of pearls with musk, saffron, aloe, sandal; floor of diamonds and rubies with a companion on a jeweled bed; siddhi powers; a sultan with armies and throne) and the rahao 'har bin jeeo jal bal jaao, mai apna gur pooch dekhiaa avar naahee thaao'.
Sri Rag's association with evening and seriousness is traditional; confirm.
'Near the very start of the main body' refers to Sri Rag beginning on ang 14.

Reviewer (2026-10-01): hook no longer says 'you know the feeling' or 'Guru Nanak knew that feeling too, in a sixteenth-century version' (date and inner state not in the text); removed the superlative 'most beautiful house'; practice no longer assumes the listener sits with the One. Keeper may confirm this is the first shabad of Sri Rag.
